title: Stabilizer codes over general phase spaces
abstract: We develop a theory of stabilizer codes whose stabilizer groups consist of commuting qudit Paulis, oscillator displacements, and/or planar-rotor displacements. We consider codes whose stabilizer groups form generalized lattices in quantum phase space, a condition that guarantees a finite logical dimension. We construct oscillator-rotor, rotor-qudit, and oscillator-rotor-qubit codes that cannot be decomposed into separate subsystems by generalized Clifford transformations. We also introduce an oscillator-qubit code arising from a partially lifted Golay code, where Construction A is applied to half of the Golay code coordinates. We derive analytical forms of logical operators from the symplectic dual lattice, determine Clifford-Gaussian gates from lattice symmetries, show that the code dimension equals the covolume of the stabilizer lattice, and organize the syndrome subspaces into a vector bundle. Our technique builds on earlier non-commutative geometric results by Rieffel, but it can often be interpreted simply as concatenating a given stabilizer code with a Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code, applying conventional lattice-theoretic results, and unconcatenating. We formulate distances, optimal decoding, and quantum weight enumerators, recovering the Pauli, qudit, and GKP versions together with known MacWilliams identities. We construct finite-energy codewords whose encoding is an isometry up to an error exponentially small in the inverse damping parameter.
summary: This paper develops a unified mathematical theory for stabilizer codes defined over complex quantum phase spaces combining qudit, oscillator, and rotor degrees of freedom. By employing tools from non-commutative geometry, the authors establish that the code dimension is determined by the lattice covolume. This framework unifies several known quantum error-correcting codes into a single, powerful mathematical structure.
main_problem: Developing a unified theory for stabilizer codes whose stabilizer groups are formed by commuting qudit Paulis, oscillator displacements, and/or planar-rotor displacements.
main_result: The authors construct Generalized LCA (GLCA) codes that unify existing code types (like GKP and Pauli codes) by treating them uniformly within a framework based on generalized lattices in quantum phase space.
method: The theory utilizes Rieffel's non-commutative geometry framework, treating the code structure via isotropic lattices in the quantum phase space and relating code properties to the covolume of the stabilizer lattice.
model_or_system: The system is defined on a generalized phase space $G = M 	imes \hat{M}$, where $M$ is a Locally Compact Abelian (LCA) group combining components from qudits ($\mathbb{Z}_c$), oscillators ($\mathbb{R}^p$), and planar rotors ($\mathbb{Z}_q$).
key_observables: Code dimension ($K$), logical operators, code distance, and quantum weight enumerators.
important_parameters: The structure of the stabilizer lattice $D$ relative to the phase space $G$, and the damping parameter for finite-energy codewords.
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to cases where the stabilizer group $D$ forms a lattice with a compact quotient $G/D$, ensuring a finite logical dimension.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the phase spaces for the three system types (qudit, planar rotor, oscillator) and how hybrid codes couple these types via stabilizer lattices. Table I provides a dictionary mapping code concepts to noncommutative geometry terms.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the general mathematical framework (Rieffel's module, direct integrals) to establish the code dimension via lattice theory (Pfaffians and covolume) and concludes by applying this unified theory to derive properties like logical operators and error correction measures for various hybrid code types.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, mathematically rigorous generalization of stabilizer codes that naturally incorporates continuous (oscillator) and discrete (qudit/rotor) degrees of freedom, which is highly relevant for modeling physical quantum systems.
